propositions.text: The claimant is a citizen of El Salvador alleging Convention refugee and person in need of protection status under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: The claimant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, is a citizen of El Salvador. Ms. XXXXXXX is alleging that she is a "Convention refugee" and a "person in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The claimant from El Salvador alleges refugee and protection status under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1), court states.

propositions.text: The claimant met her future husband at 14 and lived with him without parental permission.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that she met her future husband when she was 14 years old and that she went to live with him without her parents' permission.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says she met her future husband at 14 and lived with him without parental permission.

propositions.text: Her husband started beating her the same year; she stayed because she had no support.
propositions.quote: He started to beat her that same year. She stayed with him because she had no other support.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says her husband began beating her the same year and she stayed due to lack of support.

propositions.text: In 2002, her Canadian citizen husband decided to come to Canada; she followed him.
propositions.quote: She stated that, in 2002, since her husband is a Canadian citizen, he decided to come here to live; she followed him.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says in 2002 her Canadian citizen husband decided to come to Canada and she followed him.

propositions.text: They stayed in Mexico 1.5 years to save money for their trip.
propositions.quote: They stayed in Mexico for one and a half years in order to save up enough money to continue their trip.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says they stayed in Mexico 1.5 years to save money for their trip.

propositions.text: She was detained in Arizona as a minor, reunited with spouse in LA, lived in Boston where son was born in 2004, married in 2005, then came to Canada.
propositions.quote: When she arrived in the United States, she was detained in Arizona because she was a minor. She then met up with her spouse again in Los Angeles. They then went to live in Boston, where her son was born on XXXXXXX, 2004. They were married on XXXXX, 2005, and then came to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says she was detained in Arizona, reunited with spouse in LA, lived in Boston where son was born, married in 2005, then came to Canada.

propositions.text: They entered Canada in 2005 with temporary authorization as spouse of Canadian citizen.
propositions.quote: They were driven to the Canadian border, and she entered on XXXXXXX, 2005, with a temporary authorization, since she was the spouse of a Canadian citizen.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says she entered Canada in 2005 with temporary authorization as spouse of Canadian citizen.

propositions.text: They lived with husband's mother; husband was often out, used drugs, abused her, left for a month with another woman, neglected her and son.
propositions.quote: They lived with her husband's mother, but her husband went out often, used drugs and abused her. One day, he left for a month with another woman and no longer looked after her and her son.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says they lived with husband's mother; husband was often out, used drugs, abused her, left for a month with another woman, neglected her and son.

propositions.text: Husband beat her badly; she went to CLSC; he broke glass door with her head and beat her with cable; she feared police and shelter.
propositions.quote: Another day, he beat her badly. She went to a CLSC. He broke a glass door with her head and beat her with an electrical cable. She stated that she did not call the police because she was afraid and that she did not go to the women's shelter because she was told that it was like a prison and she did not need care.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says husband beat her badly, she went to CLSC, he broke glass door with her head, beat her with cable; she feared police and shelter.

propositions.text: In 2008, husband tried to beat her; she left without child; he refused visitation; she found shelter and learned he cannot forbid visitation.
propositions.quote: In XXXXX 2008, her husband tried to beat her and she had to leave without her child. He then refused to let her see him. She finally ended up at a women's shelter with her child, and she found out that he did not have the right to forbid her from seeing her child.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says in 2008 husband tried to beat her; she left without child; he refused visitation; she found shelter and learned he cannot forbid visitation.

propositions.text: She received deportation letter, did not know status, feared returning to El Salvador.
propositions.quote: She found out that she had received a deportation letter, but she did not know what her status was. She was afraid of returning to her country.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says she received deportation letter, did not know status, feared returning to El Salvador.

propositions.text: She claimed refugee protection in 2008, three years after arriving in Canada.
propositions.quote: She claimed refugee protection in XXXXX 2008-three years after she arrived in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says she claimed refugee protection in 2008, three years after arriving in Canada.

propositions.text: The panel finds claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection after analyzing evidence.
propositions.quote: Having analyzed the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection".

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection after analyzing evidence.

propositions.text: The panel is satisfied as to claimant's identity based on passport and birth certificate photocopies.
propositions.quote: Given the documents submitted as evidence,1 namely, the photocopies of her passport, which was valid from XXXXXX, 2005, to XXXXXX, 2010, and of her birth certificate, which is in her possession, the panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity.

paragraphs.summary: The panel is satisfied as to claimant's identity based on passport and birth certificate photocopies.

propositions.text: The claimant's testimony about fears if returned to El Salvador was not credible.
propositions.quote: The claimant's testimony was not credible regarding her alleged fears should she return to El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's testimony about fears if returned to El Salvador not credible.

propositions.text: Claimant testified about meeting spouse in El Salvador, his Canadian citizenship, their living arrangements and marriage timeline.
propositions.quote: During her testimony, the claimant explained that she met her spouse, XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXX, in El Salvador when he was there on vacation. He is a Canadian citizen but was born in El Salvador. He allegedly went to the United States with his parents when he was around two years old and came to Canada later. She started living with him when she was 14 and he was 26. Sometime around 2003, they decided to come to Canada. She allegedly followed him to Mexico. He allegedly left her there for her to cross the border while he supposedly waited for her in the United States. After arriving in that country, she met her spouse in Los Angeles and gave birth to their son in Boston on XXXXXXX, 2004. They were married on XXXXX, 2005, before coming to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The panel recounts claimant's testimony about meeting spouse, his citizenship, living arrangements, and marriage timeline.

propositions.text: Panel is surprised claimant stayed 14 months in US without claiming asylum; explanations vague.
propositions.quote: The panel is surprised that she stayed in the United States for 14 months, from XXXX 2004 to XXXXXXX 2005, without attempting to claim asylum. Her explanations on that topic are vague.

paragraphs.summary: The panel is surprised claimant stayed 14 months in US without claiming asylum; explanations vague.

propositions.text: Panel accepts claimant's explanation for not claiming asylum in US due to young age, abuse, and following Canadian spouse.
propositions.quote: Given the claimant's young age at the time and the possibility that she was abused, as she alleged, the panel accepts her explanations for not claiming asylum in the United States because she was following her spouse, who later became her husband, and because, since he is Canadian, she was considering coming to Canada, her husband's country of residence.

paragraphs.summary: Panel accepts claimant's explanation for not claiming asylum in US due to young age, abuse, and following Canadian spouse.

propositions.text: Panel questions why claimant waited three years to claim refugee protection in Canada.
propositions.quote: However, the panel wants to understand why the claimant waited three years to claim refugee protection in Canada.

propositions.text: Claimant entered Canada in 2005 with temporary permit as spouse of Canadian citizen.
propositions.quote: In fact, she entered Canada on XXXXXXX, 2005, with a temporary permit because she is married to a Canadian.

propositions.text: Claimant said husband told her he would sponsor her; she did not check status due to abuse.
propositions.quote: She explained that he told her that he would apply to sponsor her, but that having lived under the yoke of her violent ex-husband for many years, she did not check her status at the time.

propositions.text: Husband became more violent in Canada, used drugs, abused her; she bled and saw CLSC doctor but submitted no documents.
propositions.quote: Her spouse supposedly became more violent after they arrived in Canada. Allegedly, he was often away, used drugs and hit her often. On one of these occasions, he allegedly shoved her hard against a door and hit her on the legs and in the face. She allegedly bled and went to see a doctor at the CLSC, but she did not submit any documents on this subject.

propositions.text: Claimant did not submit CLSC documents because she did not know she was supposed to.
propositions.quote: Questioned as to why she did not submit any documents from the CLSC, the claimant replied that she did not know that, that she did not know that she was supposed to do that.

propositions.text: Date of CLSC incident unclear; claimant gave vague and contradictory dates for visits.
propositions.quote: The date of this incident is difficult to establish. She replied that it happened before she left the house, around XXXXXXX 2008. However, the claimant mentioned at one point that she went to the CLSC a number of times. Once again, the dates of the visits are vague. She stated that her first visit occurred during the same month she left the house and then stated that it was in XXXXXXX 2008. She later stated that it started around 2007.

paragraphs.summary: The panel questions why claimant waited three years to claim protection; notes abuse, no CLSC documents, and vague dates.

propositions.text: Panel surprised by failure to submit CLSC evidence and contradictions about incidents.
propositions.quote: The failure to submit evidence to support the fact that she went to the CLSC, as well as the contradictions regarding the incidents that took place, surprises the panel.

paragraphs.summary: The panel is surprised by claimant's failure to submit CLSC evidence and contradictions about incidents.

propositions.text: The panel is surprised by the alleged visits to the CLSC and doctor and the domestic violence allegations due to confusion and lack of documents.
propositions.quote: The panel is surprised by the alleged visits to the CLSC and to the doctor and, consequently, by the allegations of domestic violence that she experienced.

propositions.text: The claimant did not submit documents from the CLSC to show four or five interviews or treatment and gave no real explanation.
propositions.quote: she did not submit any documents from the CLSC to show that she had four or five interviews, as alleged, and received treatment. Furthermore, she provided no real explanation for this.

propositions.text: The claimant has been in Quebec for three years and is assisted by several lawyers for divorce and refugee claim.
propositions.quote: She has, however, been in Quebec for three years and is being assisted by several lawyers, for, among other things, her divorce and her refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant's alleged CLSC visits and domestic violence claims surprising due to confusion and lack of documents, noting she has legal assistance in Quebec.

propositions.text: Only after the deportation order in 2008 did the claimant take steps like leaving husband, claiming refugee protection, going to shelter, and starting divorce.
propositions.quote: it was only after the deportation order was issued on XXXXXXX, 2008, that the claimant took certain steps, including leaving her husband in XXXXXX 2008 and claiming refugee protection in XXXXXXX 2008.

propositions.text: She went to a battered women's shelter and started divorce proceedings in 2008; divorce finalized in 2010 due to increasing violence.
propositions.quote: She went to a shelter for battered women on XXXXXXX, 2008, and started divorce proceedings on XXXXXXX, 2008. Her divorce was finalized on XXXXX, 2010-all of that because her spouse had become increasingly violent.

paragraphs.summary: The panel notes the claimant only took protective steps after the 2008 deportation order, including leaving husband, shelter stay, and divorce due to violence.

propositions.text: The panel considered documents submitted: Personal Information Form, divorce motion, divorce decree, court order against spouse, removal order.
propositions.quote: In addition to her Personal Information Form, the claimant submitted four documents to corroborate these allegations: a motion to institute divorce proceedings, her divorce decree, a court order issued against her spouse, and her removal order.

propositions.text: The panel also considered a letter from a shelter confirming claimant and son stayed there in 2008.
propositions.quote: a letter from the XXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX dated XXXXXXXX, 2008, which confirms that the claimant started staying at this shelter with her son on XXXXXXXX, 2008, and was still living there as of XXXXXXXX, 2008.

paragraphs.summary: The panel considered multiple documents including divorce papers, court order, removal order, and shelter letter confirming claimant's stay with son.

propositions.text: The panel accepts claimant was a domestic violence victim despite no police call or medical documents, acknowledging difficulties victims face.
propositions.quote: The panel accepts the claimant's allegations that she was a victim of domestic violence, even though she never called the police-she was scared-and even though she did not submit any medical documents on this subject; because victims of domestic violence can experience difficulties testifying and have memory lapses.

propositions.text: Claimant is young (born 1987) and may have problems organizing thoughts and gathering supporting documents.
propositions.quote: it is possible that the claimant, who is a young woman (born in 1987), would have some problems organizing her thoughts and gathering the documents required to support her testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The panel accepts the claimant's domestic violence victim status despite no police or medical documents, noting her youth and possible memory issues.

propositions.text: The panel finds claimant's delay in claiming refugee protection reasonable given domestic violence and young age when meeting abusive spouse.
propositions.quote: the panel considers the claimant's explanations regarding her delay in claiming refugee protection to be reasonable, given that she was a victim of domestic violence and that she was only 14 when she met this man who is 12 years her senior and that she endured living under his control and had little contact outside of her home.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds the claimant's delay in refugee claim reasonable due to domestic violence and young age when meeting abusive spouse.

propositions.text: The panel wants to know what claimant fears if returned to El Salvador since spouse lives in Canada and is Canadian.
propositions.quote: The panel wants to know what the claimant could fear should she return to El Salvador, since her spouse lives in Canada and is Canadian.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges former spouse could return to El Salvador to beat or kill her due to Canadian passport and lack of protection there.
propositions.quote: The claimant stated that if she returned to El Salvador, her former spouse could return to El Salvador at any time to beat her or even kill her, as she alleged at the hearing, because he has a Canadian passport and because there is no protection there.

paragraphs.summary: The panel questions claimant's fear of return given spouse in Canada; claimant alleges spouse could return to harm her in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Claimant never explained why spouse would want to return to El Salvador to find her; spouse was on holidays and had no fixed address.
propositions.quote: Also, the claimant never explained why her former spouse would want to return to El Salvador to find her. He was on holidays when she met him; he was XXXXXXX on a team, and they had no fixed address, as they both lived at different addresses, as stated at the hearing.

propositions.text: Spouse's entire family is in Canada except grandmother in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: The claimant also stated that her former spouse's entire family is in Canada. His grandmother is his only relative in El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant did not explain spouse's motive to return; spouse's family is mostly in Canada except grandmother.

propositions.text: Spouse has little reason to return to El Salvador; no residence there and family mostly in Canada except grandmother.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the claimant's former spouse has little reason to return to El Salvador. He obviously does not have a residence there, and all of his family is in Canada, except for his grandmother.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds spouse has little reason to return to El Salvador given no residence and family in Canada except grandmother.

propositions.text: Claimant is mother of child acknowledged by father, which could motivate finding spouse in El Salvador if she left with child.
propositions.quote: The claimant, however, is the mother of a child who has been acknowledged by the father, which could constitute a reason for trying to find his former spouse in El Salvador if she were to leave Canada with the child.

propositions.text: Father applied for Canadian citizenship for son; custody not stipulated; son has Canadian citizenship.
propositions.quote: However, the father has applied for Canadian citizenship for his son, since he is the son of a Canadian. Given that the child's custody has not been stipulated in the divorce documents and that her son has Canadian citizenship.

propositions.text: Panel opines little chance claimant would leave Canada with son given citizenship and custody status.
propositions.quote: the panel is of the opinion that there is little chance that the claimant would leave the country with her son.

paragraphs.summary: The panel finds claimant's child custody and son's Canadian citizenship make it unlikely she would leave Canada with the child.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe claimant's allegations that ex-spouse intends to threaten or kill her in El Salvador, noting he lives in Montréal with another girlfriend.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the panel does not believe the claimant's allegations that her ex-spouse intends to go to El Salvador to threaten or to kill her, particularly since she stated that he is living in Montréal with another "girlfriend".

paragraphs.summary: The panel disbelieves claimant's claim that ex-spouse intends to threaten or kill her in El Salvador, noting his life in Montréal.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimant is not credible about threats from former spouse in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: The panel concludes that the claimant is not credible regarding the alleged threats that she might experience in El Salvador from her former spouse, who lives in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes claimant is not credible about threats from former spouse in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Panel does not believe claimant would be threatened because of gender if returned to El Salvador.
propositions.quote: although the panel does not believe that the claimant would be threatened because of her gender should she return to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Panel considers claimant's young age, eight years outside El Salvador, five years in Canada, and having a son in Canada as reasons she wants to remain.
propositions.quote: the panel does consider that, given the claimant's young age, the fact that she has spent eight years outside El Salvador, that she has already lived in Canada for five years, and that she has a son in Canada, the panel understands that she would want to improve her situation and remain in Canada.

propositions.text: Panel lacks jurisdiction to grant refugee protection on humanitarian and compassionate grounds despite sympathy.
propositions.quote: despite the sympathy that the panel feels toward this claimant, it does not have the jurisdiction to grant her refugee protection status on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

paragraphs.summary: The panel does not believe claimant faces gender-based threats but understands her desire to stay; lacks jurisdiction for humanitarian protection.

propositions.text: Panel concludes claimant did not demonstrate serious possibility of persecution as member of particular social group (women) if returned to El Salvador.
propositions.quote: the panel concludes that the claimant did not demonstrate that she faces a "serious possibility" of persecution under one of the Convention grounds, that is, as a member of a particular social group-women-should she return to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Claimant did not demonstrate on balance of probabilities risk of torture, risk to life, or cruel and unusual treatment if returned.
propositions.quote: She also did not demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, should she return to El Salvador, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The panel concludes claimant failed to show serious persecution or risk of torture, death, or cruel treatment if returned to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Claimant's refugee protection claim is rejected.
propositions.quote: Consequently, her claim for refugee protection is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The panel rejects the claimant's refugee protection claim.
